newsitem.title: KENYA: Coffee prices seen steady in Uganda,lower in Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices seen steady in Uganda,lower in Kenya.

text.p: Coffee prices will continue their decline for a fourth week at Kenya's export auction next week but should hold steady in Uganda, traders said on Friday.
They said a major factor of low prices was a declining international market but local factors were also present.
A senior trader said prices at the Nairobi auction next Tuesday were expected to drift $3-5 lower mainly on a declining terminal market and weakening of other differentials.
The trader said quality remained "reasonable" but was seen declining in the week after next. He said quantities were on a decline on insufficient stocks from the Coffee Board of Kenya.
"The Coffee Board will offer for auction only 33,000 60-kg next week from 40,000 bags this week," he said.
A trader from a leading coffee house said quality at around this time was always on the lower side but "good enough".

"The current late crop is usually lower in quality and prices cannot match the main crop, so we are always down at this stage," the trader said. "With New York down as well and on a downward trend, we can only be expected to follow."
"Unless something miraculous happens, we should be lower at the next week's auction," the trader added.
A senior coffee player said the decline in quantities on offer may be as a result of a wrangle over marketing between the Coffee Board of Kenya and other agencies.
The player singled out Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union, the main miller, as leading the campaign to have the board relinguish its marketing role and assume regulatory work.

"As the main miller and with this wrangle, perhaps the Union has not given in enough coffee for auctioning. Stocks have declined although the market view is that the stocks should begin a rise pretty soon again," the player added.
At this week's auction, prices fell by as much as $7.

A senior official from the Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd said the market was much weaker. Premium grade AAs averaged $133 per 50 kg bag from $138.50, grade ABs fell to $124 from $132 while grade Cs eased to $122 from 129.
"For a third week the market declined. There was very little price variation between the main grades," an official said.
In Kampala, a senior trader said prices were on average $230 lower on London November and January "where they have held for some time now".

The trader said the state agency Uganda Coffee Development Authority and private Uganda Coffee Trade Federation were quite happy with prices in that range because they represented what the bodies saw as "adequate costing".

Another Kampala trader said rains in growing areas were delaying coffee drying, which should ordinarily take six days, by up to two weeks "and delaying the entire process of getting the coffee on to the market".
But he added that the crop from the central regions had started coming through and quality was seen improving.
"Now we shall continue observing London and hope it makes gains, then we are likely to follow."
